# The optimization problem

For $n$ experimental units, let $\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^n$ be the observed
responses and let the $n\times p$ design matrix $\mathbf X$ contain the
predictors used by the model. The linear mean model is

$$
\mathbf y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,
\qquad
\operatorname{E}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid\mathbf X)=\mathbf 0.
$$

Ordinary least squares (OLS) chooses the coefficient vector whose fitted values
are closest to $\mathbf y$ in squared Euclidean distance:

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\arg\min_{\mathbf b}\|\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b\|_2^2.
$$

The model space is the column space $\mathcal C(\mathbf X)$: every possible
fitted vector $\mathbf X\mathbf b$ lies in this subspace of $\mathbb R^n$.
Least squares is therefore a projection problem, not just an algebraic recipe.

The rows of $\mathbf X$ represent experimental units. In an RNA-expression
study, those units might be independent patients; reads, cells from the same
patient, or repeated technical measurements do not become independent rows
merely because software can store them that way.

# Normal equations and orthogonal projection

Write the residual vector as $\mathbf e=\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b$. Expanding
the residual sum of squares and differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\mathbf b}
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b)^\mathsf T
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b)
=-2\mathbf X^\mathsf T(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b).
$$

At a minimum,

$$
\boxed{\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf y},
\qquad
\boxed{\mathbf X^\mathsf T\hat{\mathbf e}=\mathbf 0}.
$$

Thus the residual is orthogonal to every design column. If $\mathbf X$ has full
column rank,

$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf y.
$$

The fitted vector is

$$
\hat{\mathbf y}=\mathbf H\mathbf y,
\qquad
\mathbf H=\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\mathsf T.
$$

The hat matrix is symmetric and idempotent:
$\mathbf H^\mathsf T=\mathbf H$ and $\mathbf H^2=\mathbf H$. These are the
defining algebraic properties of an orthogonal projector. The residual-maker
$\mathbf M=\mathbf I-\mathbf H$ is also symmetric and idempotent, with
$\hat{\mathbf e}=\mathbf M\mathbf y$.

Because the fitted and residual vectors are orthogonal,

$$
\|\mathbf y\|_2^2
=\|\hat{\mathbf y}\|_2^2+\|\hat{\mathbf e}\|_2^2.
$$

With an intercept, the same geometry applied after centering yields the familiar
decomposition

$$
\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2
=\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2+\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2.
$$

This identity is exact in the fitted sample. It does not show that the mean
function is correct, that the predictors are causal, or that the model will
predict new observations well.

# What full rank means

Full column rank means that no design column is an exact linear combination of
the others. It gives a unique coefficient vector. If rank is deficient, fitted
values can still be unique while individual coefficients are not: several
vectors $\mathbf b$ produce the same point in $\mathcal C(\mathbf X)$.

Common causes include an intercept plus indicators for every category, a batch
indicator identical to treatment, or more fitted coefficients than independent
units. Near-linear dependence does not destroy uniqueness, but it creates long,
flat directions in the least-squares surface. Small changes in the data can then
produce large coefficient changes.

The projection should not be computed by explicitly forming
$(\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf X)^{-1}$. Forming the cross-product squares the
condition number. QR factorization is the standard stable route for a full-rank
problem; singular-value decomposition exposes rank and ill-conditioned
directions directly.

# Residualization and the Frisch--Waugh--Lovell result

Partition the design as $\mathbf X=[\mathbf X_1\;\mathbf x_2]$, and let

$$
\mathbf M_1=\mathbf I-
\mathbf X_1(\mathbf X_1^\mathsf T\mathbf X_1)^{-1}\mathbf X_1^\mathsf T.
$$

The coefficient of $\mathbf x_2$ in the full regression is

$$
\boxed{
\hat\beta_2
=\frac{\mathbf x_2^\mathsf T\mathbf M_1\mathbf y}
{\mathbf x_2^\mathsf T\mathbf M_1\mathbf x_2}
}.
$$

To see the result, minimize over $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ for any fixed $b_2$.
The remaining residual is
$\mathbf M_1(\mathbf y-\mathbf x_2b_2)$; differentiating its squared length
with respect to $b_2$ gives the displayed expression.

Geometrically, first remove from both $\mathbf y$ and $\mathbf x_2$ the
components explained linearly by $\mathbf X_1$. The slope between those two
residual vectors is the full-model coefficient. A coefficient therefore uses
only predictor variation orthogonal to the other design columns. If almost no
such variation remains, the denominator is small and the estimate is unstable.

# Leverage and influence in the projection

The diagonal element $h_{ii}$ of $\mathbf H$ is the leverage of unit $i$:

$$
\hat y_i=\sum_{j=1}^n h_{ij}y_j,
\qquad
0\le h_{ii}\le 1,
\qquad
\sum_i h_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf H)=p.
$$

High leverage means that a row of the design is unusual in predictor space. It
does not by itself imply a large residual or an error. Influence combines
leverage with outcome disagreement: a high-leverage unit whose response follows
the fitted pattern may change the coefficients little, whereas a high-leverage
unit with a large residual can dominate them.

Under homoskedastic errors,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat e_i\mid\mathbf X)=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii}),
$$

so raw residuals have different variances even when the original errors do not.
Studentized residuals account for this geometric fact. Cook's distance and
DFBETAs then quantify how deleting a unit changes the fitted vector or a
particular coefficient. Deletion diagnostics are sensitivity analyses, not
automatic rules for discarding inconvenient observations.

# Weighted geometry

If the conditional error covariance is known up to scale as
$\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid\mathbf X)=\sigma^2\mathbf V$,
generalized least squares minimizes

$$
(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b)^\mathsf T
\mathbf V^{-1}(\mathbf y-\mathbf X\mathbf b).
$$

This is ordinary projection after whitening by a matrix $\mathbf L$ satisfying
$\mathbf L^\mathsf T\mathbf L=\mathbf V^{-1}$. Weighted least squares is the
diagonal special case. The choice of weights changes the metric and therefore
the projection; weights should encode a justified variance or sampling model,
not merely shrink observations that fit poorly.

# A small worked geometry

Fit an intercept and a centered predictor
$\mathbf x=(-1,0,1)^\mathsf T$ to
$\mathbf y=(1,2,6)^\mathsf T$. Orthogonality of the intercept and centered
predictor gives

$$
\hat\beta_0=\bar y=3,
\qquad
\hat\beta_1=\frac{\mathbf x^\mathsf T\mathbf y}
{\mathbf x^\mathsf T\mathbf x}=\frac{5}{2}.
$$

Hence $\hat{\mathbf y}=(0.5,3,5.5)^\mathsf T$ and
$\hat{\mathbf e}=(0.5,-1,0.5)^\mathsf T$. Direct calculation confirms
$\mathbf 1^\mathsf T\hat{\mathbf e}=0$ and
$\mathbf x^\mathsf T\hat{\mathbf e}=0$. The normal equations are visible as
right angles.

# Bioinformatics design example

Suppose 48 independent donor samples are assayed for a pathway score. The design
contains an intercept, treatment, age, sex, and sequencing batch. Each column is
a direction in donor-level observation space. The adjusted treatment coefficient
uses only the treatment direction remaining after its projection on the other
columns.

If all treated donors were processed in batch B and all controls in batch A,
treatment and batch point in the same design direction. Their separate effects
are not identified. More reads or repeated libraries cannot create the missing
donor-level contrast. If treatment and batch are merely highly associated, the
contrast exists but is short, so uncertainty is large and estimates are
sensitive to a few donors.

The statistical statement is about an adjusted mean contrast on the pathway-score
scale under the model. Biological interpretation additionally depends on donor
selection, tissue composition, assay normalization, effect magnitude, and
external replication.

# Assumptions and sensitivity checks

| Issue | Geometric symptom | Consequence | Check or response |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rank deficiency | Redundant design directions | Coefficients not unique | Inspect design rank and estimable contrasts; redesign or reparameterize |
| Near collinearity | Very small singular values | Large coefficient variance | Inspect singular values and partial predictor spread; report sensitivity |
| Nonlinear mean | Residual pattern outside the chosen model space | Projection is a misleading summary | Residual and partial-residual plots; add justified transformations or splines |
| Unequal variance | Error ellipsoid not spherical | Classical standard errors are wrong or inefficient | Plot residual spread; use justified variance modeling or robust covariance |
| Dependence | Off-diagonal error covariance | Ordinary uncertainty is too small or otherwise wrong | Respect sampling hierarchy; use cluster, mixed, or generalized least-squares methods |
| Influential units | High leverage combined with large residual | Fit depends on few units | Verify records and report transparent deletion or robust-fit sensitivity |

# Connections and take-home messages

- [Simple linear regression](simple-linear-regression.qmd) introduces the
  one-predictor model.
- [Multiple linear regression](multiple-linear-regression.qmd) develops adjusted
  coefficients and omitted-variable reasoning.
- [Regression uncertainty and coefficient interpretation](regression-uncertainty-and-coefficient-interpretation.qmd)
  connects this geometry to standard errors, contrasts, and prediction.
- [Standard errors](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd) explains
  repeated-sampling uncertainty more generally.
- [Sensitivity analysis and robustness](../statistical-inference/sensitivity-analysis-and-robustness.qmd)
  provides a broader framework for assumption checks.

1. OLS projects the response onto the column space of the design matrix.
2. The normal equations say that the residual is orthogonal to every included
   design direction.
3. Full rank identifies coefficients; small singular values reveal unstable
   directions even when a unique solution exists.
4. Partial-regression geometry shows exactly which predictor variation estimates
   an adjusted coefficient.
5. The geometry is a sample identity. Scientific interpretation and valid
   uncertainty still require assumptions about design, errors, and experimental
   units.
